newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-BUILDERS STILL SHAPING WIMBLEDON'S FUTURE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BUILDERS STILL SHAPING WIMBLEDON'S FUTURE.

text.p: "If you want the debenture lounge, turn right at the skip," said the security guard, standing in front of a building site which used to be the venue for the world's most famous tennis championships.

A Japanese tourist also standing on the pavement outside the All England Club looked rather doubtful. If he returns to queue up with the rest of the public in June, Wimbledon officials hope he will be far more impressed by what he finds.

In the past, the words "innovative" and "bold" have not been closely associated with those in charge at Wimbledon, but the ambitious redevelopment of the All England Club could turn out to be their finest hour.

There was understandable dismay when the old number one court was pensioned off last year, 72 years of tennis memories failing to deter the bulldozers. In its place, unless a monsoon interrupts the building work, spectators will find something refreshingly different.
The committee have embarked on what they call "the most exciting development" since the All England Club was relocated in 1922.
A new stadium with 11,000 clear-view seats, an increase of 4,500 on its predecessor and two more brand-new grass courts will be the most obvious changes for this year's visitors.

Stage two, to be ready in time for the 2000 championships, will also incorporate a new facilities building for players, officials and the press on the site of the old number one court, with a remodelling of number two court to follow.

This may sound similar to many of the world's other leading tennis venues, and indeed those of other other sports. In London alone, Lord's cricket ground has had the bulldozers in over the winter and Wembley is also poised for a massive redevelopment.
Where Wimbledon is striving to be original is the emphasis on creating what chief executive Chris Gorringe likes to describe as "Tennis in an English Country Garden."

This was a little hard to visualise standing on a draughty hillside watching mechanical diggers splashing across the muddy site below, but the aim is to give picnicking spectators enviable views across the grounds and beyond.

The players will eventually have their own private lawned area leading to a walkway which will take them above the heads of the public to their changing-rooms. Most crucially of all for the traditionalist, there will even be an extra number of places to buy strawberries.

Giving the crowds what they want, of course, would be irrelevant without the help of the players, although club chairman John Curry was unrepentant on Thursday about the committee's decision not to award equal prizemoney in the men's and women's events.
"Every night I go outside the gates and ask the public for their opinions. What they still say is that they prefer the men's matches to the women's."
This unscientific poll also suggests Wimbledon spectators are not too concerned about the 'two-shot rallies' which have raised concerns that grass is too helpful to the big servers.
"Other than Agassi, the most popular player is Goran Ivanisevic," revealed Curry. And the most unpopular? "There are no unpopular players here."

This year's championships will thus see no changes in ball or racket technology, relying instead on a subtle shift of scenery to enhance the drama. In fact, the new stadium court looks uncannily like Centre Court, right down to the familiar ivy-green decor.

Its first test, somewhat bizarrely, will be as a venue for a June recording of the BBC religious programme "Songs of Praise", ensuring the first service on the court will be delivered by a vicar instead of Tim Henman.

And what about any of the 550 workmen involved in building the new court who fancy watching some tennis this summer? Unless they dig a secret access tunnel, they will have to queue up like everyone else.
